Madam Speaker, I rise today to lend my voice in resolute opposition to the reinstatement of capital punishment. Though it is always a privilege to speak to the nation and to my constituents in this Chamber, it is with sadness that I am now compelled to do so on this issue.
It is a tragedy that the ugly issue of state execution should once again be brought before this House. It is obvious that the Government has taken this opportunity to use this debate in an attempt to distract attention from the great many problems facing Canadians as a result of the Government's incompetence.
It is my feeling that the call for the reinstatement of capital punishment is an understandable but illogical reaction to the brutality that we see all too often in Canada. I am certain that every Canadian is enraged and disgusted at the thought of criminals such as Clifford Olson and the horrible acts he has committed. It is in reaction to big headlines that people's attitudes toward crime are formed. Their fears are understandable, but I believe somewhat exaggerated.
June 29, 1987

According to a 1982 study carried out by the University of Toronto's Centre of Criminology, almost 75 per cent of Canadians believe that violent crimes make up about one-third of all crimes committed. The reality is that violent crimes account for only 5.7 per cent of the total. Moreover, almost two-thirds of Canadians believe that the murder rate has increased since the abolition of capital punishment in 1976. However, a report from the Solicitor General's department has shown that the rate has reflected no significant changes. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), when he spoke the other night, reinforced that argument.
In the year prior to the complete abolition of capital punishment there were 701 homicides in Canada, a rate of 3.09 per 100,000 citizens. In 1986 that rate had dropped to 2.87. Obviously, misinformation has created a great deal of panic in the population.
It is the duty of every Member of this House to speak clearly and directly to Canadians. I am sure that as people follow this debate it will become abundantly clear that capital punishment is both unnecessary and unjustifiable. Much will be said about the responsibilities of Members of this House to their constituents, to the nation as a whole, and, indeed, to their own consciences. It is my belief that the needs of my constituents is the most important concern I have to address. It is the needs of one's constituents that must take priority.
However, it is important to separate what is needed from what is merely desired. We have all seen polls, and Members who spoke prior to me mentioned this, that indicate that a majority of Canadians want to return to capital punishment. Since the public has been misinformed, it is not our duty here to follow the demands of the public. On the contrary, it is our responsibility to make use of this debate to try to educate the public and to show rational and moral leadership in maintaining the abolition of capital punishment. We must assume the confidence of our constituents and move forward according to our judgment. If this is not done and Members of the House turn instead to vote in a manner designed only to meet the demands of the polls, then Parliament will have dealt a great blow to the progress of the country. The cycle of revenge will have begun.
It is the tradition of our justice system to provide three functions in its work. Punishment must be a deterrent. It must be a form of retribution and it must encourage rehabilitation. Capital punishment falls hopelessly short of meeting any of those three required principles. The evidence and statistics relating to the death penalty as a deterrent are completely clear-capital punishment is not a deterrent.
I fail to see what overwhelming deterrent effect can be created by institutionalized killings. What example can be achieved? Are we showing people what to expect if they take another's life, or are we setting an example of how to react when one is wronged? State executions of criminals hardly seem like an effective method to show how wrong it is to kill.
Capital Punishment
It is hard to argue that the death penalty is not a decisive form of retribution. Some will claim it is the ultimate retribution. The problem here is that dead criminals cannot be rehabilitated. Since there is no rehabilitation, the entire society loses something. A lost life will never again contribute to society. The execution of a criminal has never brought a victim back to life. Capital punishment can add nothing but revenge to society. Under any careful examination there is no way to interpret it as a positive step.
When I was born in Freeland, Prince Edward Island, I was immediately given and privileged with all the rights, freedoms and liberties to which the citizens of this great country of ours are entitled. Of course, I was also instantly subject to the laws of the nation.
No one would dispute the right of the Government to remove a person's right to freedom within a society if that person has committed a crime. Prison sentences remove the criminal element of society. These people have forfeited rights they once held. However, the right to life is something that no government can logically or morally take away. Simply put, the Government cannot take what it has not given.
I cannot hold myself, as others have, as a leader in morality on this issue. Instead, I follow the initiative and concern expressed to me over the last few months by at least 30 different religious bodies, ranging from national organizations to tiny church groups.
I should like to thank these groups for their guidance in this most difficult issue that this Parliament is faced with. These people believe, as do I, and as do, I believe, all Canadians, in the sanctity of each and every human life.
The Canadian justice system cannot, and should not, be used by the Government as the arbiter of death. The possibilities of error are endless; and once an error is committed in this context it cannot be undone. There have been many cases in our legal history where people who were hanged were later found to be innocent, or at the very least convicted on false evidence.
We have, of course, as has been cited by many Members of Parliament, the Donald Marshall case and the John Wildman case, both of which remind us that while we do have a good justice system, it is not an infallible justice system. Other problems could and would arise within the justice system as a result of the implementation of capital punishment.
It is widely believed that jurors trying murder cases, given the choice between bringing down a verdict of guilty with a death penalty and a not guilty verdict, come down on the side of a not guilty verdict. As former Crown counsel Alan Cooper explained: "If you talk to the average guy on the street, he talks tough. But when it actually comes down to his making the decision, he won't do it."

June 29, 1987
Capital Punishment
When a jury has the opportunity to hang a man, they rarely do it; and because they do not want death sentences, the possibility-and I emphasize "the possibility"-is that some of the guilty will go free. There is always a threat with jury trials of wide-ranging inequities in terms of who is sentenced to death and who lives. Studies have shown that the death penalty has traditionally been used more frequently in cases involving racial minorities and the poor. That is something that has been brought out by other Hon. Members during the course of this debate. And this is another sad irony, because, as we have seen, it is the same people who suffer most in our society.
The death penalty is, and has been, a measure that is used to attack a symptom rather than the cause of the problems in this country. Desperation is at the root of a great deal of crime, and we should be attacking the cause. Instead, we are focusing our attention today in this Parliament on the effects of these crimes of desperation.
Certainly there are criminal acts, as we have seen, that are both horrible and unexplainable'; but, these are the exception rather than the rule. It would be impossible to expect that our justice system could completely and unerringly separate the criminal monsters from those who are nothing more than sad tragedies. If one innocent person is to die unnecessarily, as would surely happen, then we are, each and every one of us in this Chamber, to blame, and we will have lost one more precious life in the name of blind justice.
Let us hope that neither Hon. Members of this House nor the public at large have any doubts about the result of the return to capital punishment. The fact is, some people will die: people who may have been falsely convicted; people who are consumed with guilt and who long for repentance; people who are, and who were at the time of their crime, without any control of their minds. In fact, who can say that any man who kills another in a civilized world is not insane?
There will also, undoubtedly, be people who die who could have enriched us, helped us, and even taught us many things, after a sufficient time of imprisonment, leading to repentance and rehabilitation. History is full of great men and women who spent a part or even much of their lives imprisoned, only to return as functioning and contributing members of society.
In our own nation, we have the example of Roger Caron, a man referred to by his fellow prisoners as "mad dog", who returned to society to educate and warn our youth and to advocate fair treatment of the inmates of our prisons. I ask Hon. Members, are we really so morally bankrupt as a nation, so resigned to our inability to rehabilitate people and so thirsty for revenge and spectacle that we should return to the death penalty? I certainly hope not. As a nation, we have traditionally strived to better the fate of our fellow human beings. We are recognized as a world leader in the fight for human rights.
We certainly have nothing to gain in joining such countries as South Africa and Chile, which have institutionalized and advocated capital punishment as a practical measure to curb unrest in their societies.
The problems of this country have always been solved through knowledge, hard work, and compassion. It is our duty to help the victims of crime in as many ways as possible; but it is also our duty to punish and rehabilitate the criminals themselves. It may well be that we need judicial reform. I, for one, would advocate stronger judicial reform. It is difficult to see a person who has been charged and convicted of first-degree murder out on parole after only a very few short years.
This Parliament, before going to capital punishment, the taking of the life of an individual, should try at least one other method, that being a stronger and more effective sentencing regime. We certainly do not need a justice system based on revenge.
It will be said in this House that we should return to the death penalty as a measure of government cost-saving. We hear that argument being put forth by people across this country. People say that it costs a great deal of money to keep these people incarcerated. This argument is also false. As well, it is disturbing. A study by the State of New York has shown that there is no money to be saved by executing criminals. The long line of appeals that accompany a death sentence more than offsets the money spent on the incarceration of the criminal. Quite apart from that, it is revolting to think that we could consider killing people in order to save relatively tiny sums of money; or, for that matter, any sum of money.
Perhaps those who use this argument would consider letting people starve to death-another good way of saving dollars. The Government would be better using this precious time, I believe, to implement a fairer tax system, if money is the main issue.
In closing, I should like to urge Hon. Members to look deep into their hearts to find their position on this grave issue. I think the immorality of the death penalty will be easy to see. I urge Hon. Members to feel the weight of their consciences, as I have. If we reinstate capital punishment, we will be doing so on behalf of all Canadians, and any executions which follow will be carried out in the names of a people who deeply believe in the sanctity of life.
I urge Hon. Members to think of the logic being applied here. Does it make any sense to kill to show the wrongness of killing? I do not think so.
I will be voting against the motion, and I will be doing so with a clear mind and a hopeful heart.
I should like to conclude with a quote from a letter I received from one of my concerned constituents, a Mr. Carroll Kadey, from Ellerslie, P.E.I., who has mindfully stated the truth of this issue. I quote:
For one human being to take the life of another is a great tragedy.
For society to execute a human being is barbarity.
I have stood for Parliament in two elections, 1980 and 1984, Mr. Speaker. When asked my position on capital punishment, when asked whether I would vote for the return of the death
June 29, 1987

penalty in Canada, I said, on the occasion of both campaigns, that I could not.
Last evening I attended a state dinner in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, which was hosted by one of our cabinet Ministers, the Hon. Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), and had an opportunity to have a long chat with the former Member for Egmont, the Hon. David MacDonald, who is now Canada's Ambassador to Ethiopia. My position has been clear for many years, and it was reinforced when a poll was taken on who would vote for and who would vote against the reinstatement of capital punishment. Mr. MacDonald said that he was glad to see me voting against the reinstatement of capital punishment. He said that he had done the same on many occasions, and that previous Members of Parliament for Egmont were also abolitionists. I informed him that I had read his speeches in Hansard, which he gave over the years with great consideration and care, and that I took much from them.
As did other Hon. Members, I asked the following question in my householder: "Are you for or are you against capital punishment". In my riding of Egmont I sent out 18,000 householders, and I received back something less than 200. The breakdown was something like 102 against reinstatement of capital punishment and 96 for its reinstatement.
I understand that Members of Parliament are really very concerned politically and otherwise, but there are times when we must show moral leadership. We must live with our own consciences. While we work very hard as Members of Parliament in every way we can to help our ridings and our constituents, there are some issues-and this is one of them for myself; I am also a pro-lifer-on which we must vote with our consciences. I must live with my conscience, and I hope all my constituents will understand and respect me for it.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in the debate. I suspect that for many Members of Parliament it is one of the most difficult debates which we have faced in our careers as parliamentarians and as elected leaders in our respective communities. It is not an easy debate; it is not an easy subject.
It deals with very deep-felt emotions which we experience as human beings living in this day and age. It deals with various intellectual arguments relating to something about which we as members of the human community feel very strongly, that is, our collective security or ability as individual human beings to live our lives in a society free from random violence and death. It deals with a question which affects each of us to the core regardless of political or religious beliefs, regardless of all things which separate us as human beings. This debate touches us in terms of what we share as human beings.
I am referring to the question of what we do with those in our midst who commit what is surely the most awful crime of all, that is, the taking of the life of another human being. How do we prevent that? How do we minimize it? How do we treat
Capital Punishment
those who have committed that crime? These are the questions in this debate. These are the questions which individual Members of Parliament have attempted to answer.
I should like to deal with some of the intellectual questions dealing with the logical side of the issue. Some of those who call for the restoration of capital punishment use the argument that it is a deterrent, that the state being able to put to death a murderer will deter such crime.
The truth of the matter is that that logical assertion cannot be proven. Most intelligent and reasonable people would admit that there are no statistics whatsoever to support the contention that capital punishment is a deterrent. As various speakers during the debate have pointed out, in many instances we could almost make the opposite assertion. In certain jurisdictions which have done away with capital punishment the homicide rate in fact has declined over the last number of years. The argument that it is a deterrent is not a valid one.
Another argument is that it protects society and that society needs this protection. Logically I do not think that argument holds water. Quite often, as the Law Society pointed out, the opposite can occur and the courts would be loath to convict someone of such an offence if it meant his or her execution. In certain instances a court will in fact adjudge manslaughter rather than first degree murder. Along with the notion that restoring death penalty protects society, one could also make the case that it endangers society by allowing people out who should not be allowed out.
I think the most important argument by those who want to see a return to the death penalty is the retributive justice argument, in other words, vengeance or revenge, that a member of our human family has committed such a horrifying act or acts that he or she deserves to be killed. This is perhaps the most potent of all arguments used, and I also reject it.
There is no doubt that when we read gruesome details of mass murderers like Clifford Olson that there is a certain sense of deep-rooted revulsion which we all feel, a sense of wanting to put the SOB out of his misery. We feel a sense of anger that such an awful act has been committed, that young, innocent children, at the stage of beginning to live or to discover life, have been killed by a demented animal who is a human being, a member of the human species. I think we all feel that we just want to kill the person. That part of our nature as a human being comes out, the one that wants revenge, that response of anger.
I understand that because I feel it myself. Any member of our human family will feel it. It is normal. Yet there is another part of us that calls out and helps us rise above that feeling of anger and wanting to kill for revenge. Surely that part of us that calls out is the better part of our nature. It looks at events in terms of cause and effect, of nature and seeks to understand and put reason where there was anger and pure emotion. It is that part of us that wants to make certain such things never

June 29, 1987
Capital Punishment
happen again and realizes that in order to do we must understand. That is what this debate is about, not only how we as individuals react but how we as a collective society, as a civilization, act. What part of our nature will we call forth as a community, as civilization?
In many ways this debate is a debate about how consciously leaders of our community decide what type of a civilization we will have. 1 submit that feeding emotion tonight will be an affirmation that the community called Canada tries to achieve a higher level of civilization, a higher level of conduct, one more motivated by attempting to understand rather than one of pure emotional reaction. That in large part is what this debate is about. EIow do we see ourselves as a community, as a society? How do we see ourselves as individual members of that society?
I have heard arguments that what we have to do is vote according to the wishes of our constituents. That is compelling. Practically speaking, we are all politicians and we all want to get re-elected. There is that part, of course, but there is a loftier part as well which has some validity. One attempts as a representative of the people of one's constituency to reflect the people's desires and wishes so that this, indeed, is a representative democracy. That is understandable, Mr. Speaker. But very often we have to forget that from time to time. A few weeks ago I was engaged in a radio debate over the telephone with my colleague from Saskatoon East. The Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ravis) stated that he would support capital punishment because that is what his constituents wanted. He had done his poll, and had the responses to his householders, and had decided what he was going to do.
Let me tell you about Saskatoon East, Mr. Speaker. It is a seat which the New Democratic Party represented in the previous Parliament and we will probably represent again in the next Parliament. The polls seem to indicate that the constituents in Saskatoon East want a change in their representative. I posed a question to my colleague from Saskatoon East. If I went into his riding, conducted a poll and was able to demonstrate to him that the majority of his constituents wanted him either to change Parties or resign and allow somebody else to run, would he do so. He was not quite into doing that. I told him that in a poll I would probably be able to demonstrate that the majority of his constituents were against Bill C-22, while he voted in favour of it.
I asked him would he consider, using that same argument that he was using to support capital punishment, and now vote against Bill C-22. Of course, he was not quite prepared to do that either. Our system of Government and Parliament operates in a certain way. Yes, as practical politicians and politicians wanting to represent our constituents we try to stay in tune with the desires of our constituents. We have to do more than that because there is more than that to this job. Otherwise our system of government just would not work. I suggest that the argument that you have to do what your constituents ask you to do is not a valid one.
What is it that our constituents are asking us to do? Yes, public opinion polls have shown that a 60 per cent range of the Canadian public want us to restore capital punishment. Apparently the polls also indicate people do not feel quite that strongly about it. I have detected an amazing change of mood over the last number of years.
When I fought my first election in 1972, capital punishment was a question I was asked about quite often on the doorsteps. Yet the mail I have received is by far from those who are opposed to returning capital punishment. I suspect that people are not as convinced that capital punishment is going to be the answer. I certainly feel in terms of the public impression that I get from my constituents that they are not as concerned and not as adamant now as they were before.
I suspect that most of my constituents, even those who favour restoring capital punishment, would not look kindly on me if I happened to vote according to how they want. I suspect that I will gain more support by standing here and stating what I deeply believe than if I were to change. I think our Canadian electorate is mature. I think people respect the consciousness of Members of Parliament more than they would respect one Member who would just vote according to what some poll indicated as to how he or she should vote.
The one other area on which I wish to touch is how can we make our society more secure? After all, those who want to see capital punishment restored and those who are opposed to it all agree on one thing. We want to see a safer and more secure society. We want to live our own lives with our loved ones, dependants and so forth in a more secure community. By rejecting capital punishment, it will force us to look more into the causes of violence. By not restoring capital punishment we close the door to the easy way out. We must begin to recognize the conditions that produce sick people. We must begin to examine very carefully our justice system that allows, in some cases, people who are sick to be at liberty and to commit heinous crimes again.
I remember the case of a demented person killing nurses in Saskatoon in the late 1970s. This person had a history of mental illness and sickness. He had killed farm animals and had done sick things. Yet we have devised no way as a society to keep tabs on these people, to treat these types of people, to treat them and make certain that they are never in a position to inflict harm and horror again..
Again, in the case of Clifford Olson, he was a sick person who fell between the slats of provincial and federal jurisdiction, the bureaucracy. We must examine that but we must also examine the roots of violence.
We must accept that we are living in a day and age of horrendous social, psychological, economical and technological change. Individual human lives are in freefall. Many children are being raised by single parents who are poor and have to work, come home, fix supper, change diapers and simply
June 29, 1987

physically do not have the emotional and physical strength to give love, attention, concern and all those things that make us normal human beings. A breeding ground for psychopaths is surely one way of describing the wasteland of our civilization and culture today.
Then, of course, there is the influence of the mass media and the violence and number of deaths portrayed hour after hour. Children are brought up on television, the biggest babysitter and biggest source of information right there in front of them. It gives them violence, violence, violence. Is it any wonder we produce violent people? Does anyone think that killing those violent people will solve the problem of violence? No, it will just feed on it and more violence will beget more violence.
If we are really concerned about stopping violence, we must address the question of how we can maintain individual freedom of expression and still cut down on the amount of violence to which our youngsters are exposed. By saying no to the question of capital punishment, we force ourselves to address the real causes and will hopefully achieve some solution so that we can live in a safer and sound world.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been waiting and in a sense dreading this moment for 11 years. Ever since I witnessed the last debate on capital punishment in 1976, I have wanted to place my views on the record in the House of Commons and cast my vote on this critically important albeit wrenching issue. This is the most difficult speech I have ever had to make. However, when the free vote is recorded later this day, I will vote in favour of the motion to reinstate capital punishment in principle.
I may, however, be voting from a perspective not shared by other colleagues on all sides of the House. My gut feeling tells me that we should put the death penalty back on the statute books at once. My head tells me that this country will never again see another person executed even if we do restore capital punishment in principle later tonight. Let me explain my reasons for obeying my gut instinct rather than my realistic rationale.
Eleven years ago, I sat up there in the Parliamentary Press Gallery, the third-floor balcony overlooking this place, and I listened carefully to many stirring speeches through countless hours of debate on the abolition of capital punishment. Incidentally, there were stirring speeches in 1976 but there have been very stirring speeches in 1987 as well. I commend many of my colleagues on both sides of the House for some of the profound and in some cases moving speeches that they have made.
As a television journalist for some 22 individual stations across Canada, I had to monitor the proceedings carefully. I provided filmed interviews with Members of Parliament to their hometown television channels along with commentaries reflecting the views of MPs on both sides of the death penalty issue from all sides of the House. I was exposed to all the arguments that we have been hearing during this debate and, I
Capital Punishment
will confess, as an objective journalist I felt comfortable in my officially neutral role. Still, I held the personal view that the death penalty was considered a mere formality on the statute books, a provision that no Government had used since 1962. It was certainly an ultimate solution that no Liberal administration had contemplated, nor would the Trudeau Government of the day do anything but commute any death sentence coming before it.
Back in July of 1976, the conventional wisdom in the Liberal Government and in the media of the day was that the abolitionists would almost certainly carry the vote and it turned out to be an extremely close vote, as I predict it will be tonight. However, it was anything but free back in 1976. Mr. Trudeau's Whips were on with a vengeance and all kinds of carrots were being dangled before government MPs immediately prior to the 1976 roll call on capital punishment. That brings us to the present debate and the conduct of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
I want to put on record that I can rarely recall hearing a more powerful and persuasive speech made by any Prime Minister than the one delivered by the Right Hon. Member for Manicouagan here in the House one week ago tonight. His thoughtful and obviously deeply felt address on capital punishment ranks with those contributions of Arthur Maloney and the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. I believe history will applaud the Right Hon. Prime Minister's speech regardless of the outcome of the vote tonight.
The fact that I am allowed to stand here in my place and disagree philosophically with my leader says something else about this Prime Minister. Soon after I became a Member of Parliament, I got used to hearing former Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau say that he would see to it that the issue of capital punishment would never again come before Parliament as long as he was in charge. Well, Pierre Trudeau is mercifully no longer in charge of this Parliament, not on the government side in any event, and that is another reason that I have a towering respect for this Prime Minister. He keeps his word. The capital punishment issue is indeed before Parliament. The matter will be dealt with one way or another during this Session. This highly controversial and intensely personal matter will be allowed to come to a truly free vote later tonight.
I might point out that the Right Hon. Member for Yellow-head (Mr. Clark), a former Prime Minister, also promised from 1976 onward that there would be a free vote in this House. He too will be able to participate in that vote tonight.
In any event, my own personal view back in 1976 was that capital punishment was abolished for political reasons and with the political clout of the Government of the day. My personal view in 1987 is that this House should restore the death penalty in principle but that while this Prime Minister is exerting no political pressure on his Progressive Conservative colleagues, I still have a journalist's sense of scepticism and

June 29, 1987
Capital Punishment
perhaps realism that this Government and any future Government many years down the road will not likely resort to the ultimate penalty even if the House of Commons does approve the motion in principle tonight.
Let me answer the obvious question which is: "If you think that this or any future Government will automatically commute any death sentence that comes before it, why in heaven's name don't you vote for continued abolition? Wouldn't that be more realistic?" The answer is no on two counts. First, it is because of my duty to my constituents which I consider extremely important and second, my personal responsibilities and my conscience.
To vote against this resolution would be a betrayal of the constituents of Hamilton-Wentworth. Through four successful federal election campaigns and following extensive polling of my riding recently, I am convinced that my gut feeling is totally in tune with the vast majority of the people I have the honour to represent. Just as an example of that, last fall on CHML Radio's open-line show, Mr. John Hardy got in touch with five or six Members of Parliament from the greater Hamilton-Burlington area. We were all on an open-line program where we received calls from listeners. Present were the Hon. Members for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin), Burlington (Mr. Kempling), Hamilton West (Mr. Peterson), Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), and in the absence of a Member of Parliament for Hamilton-Mountain, I represented that constituency along with Hamilton-Wentworth. The results of that poll were 75 per cent in favour of the restoration of the death penalty and 25 per cent against. I communicated those results immediately after the radio program.
Some of the arguments put forward were interesting. They included the following: "We have to consider the families of the victims, the survivors", "Capital Punishment is a deterrent", "Life does not mean life, it is only 25 years. This punishment is not severe enough". I am quoting directly from some of the people who called in on that program. Others said: "The prisons are too lax, they're too soft, they're too comfortable".
The comment of one caller in particular got to me. He was a police officer who referred to the Prime Minister's comments last fall that "emotions are too high now to have a free vote on capital punishment". Immediately after that police officer was murdered, when emotions were running so high in the House of Commons, was possibly not the time to have a free vote on capital punishment. However, the officer made the point that police officers continue to be murdered and there is no time in between these deaths to cool off.
The concerns of the people of the greater Hamilton- Wentworth region are much like mine and can best be expressed in the words of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. Here is what Canada's thirteenth Prime Minister, a long-time abolitionist, wrote in his book, One Canada:
Society must be protected from those who kill for profit or who regard murder as an occupational hazard in the commission of robberies or kidnappings.
The people of Hamilton-Wentworth and I worry about the fact that society treats the killers better than we do the victims' relatives. I can say as a former newsman that it certainly seems as though we give people who have gunned down Popes, presidents and policemen more publicity and more consideration.
There is an overwhelming impression in my part of the country that people who have murdered before are quite likely to murder again while on parole. There is a fear in my community about how people can be properly advised when these killers are back out on the street. The solution, they say, is surely not after the fact-the solution is before the fact.
My first reason for voting for this motion tonight is that I have great respect for my constituents and for their views. When we are asked to pass judgment on an issue as complex and important as this one, I have absolutely no hesitation whatsoever in asking for and relying on the guidance and advice of the people of Hamilton-Wentworth.
My personal reasons for supporting the motion do not stem from the point of view of bloody-minded revenge and retribution, although denying the "eye-for-an-eye" approach to the capital punishment question seems to mean that it is all right for a criminal to give someone the death penalty but in fact society-you or I-cannot render the same death penalty to the criminal.
Let us face it, Mr. Speaker, a great many Canadians approach this issue out of a deep-seated revenge on behalf of relatives who sorrow for the rest of their lives as a result of deliberate acts of violence against society such as blowing up an airplane, smuggling in guns to blow away prison guards, beating to death convenience store employees, gunning down policemen, shooting up banks, or bombing embassies. It is not difficult for many people to give vent to such an "eye-for-an-eye" emotion and philosophy. From those outraged by such grizzly offences you often hear: "Hanging is too good for them".
What is more difficult to accept, however, are the dispassionate, legalistic and selected biblical arguments and passages used by some organized churches, many academics, many criminal science specialists, many media people, and others who completely ignore the peoples' views on this life and death issue.
Just as I am not quoting statistics at length in these remarks-for I think statistics can be proved to use anything and manipulate any argument, as we have seen during this debate-neither will I quote the Bible to Hon. Members because the Bible can also be quoted to prove anything if you are prepared to lift the text out of context.
I am, however, a Presbyterian by upbringing and the Judaeo-Christian tradition is the major source and the wellspring of western civilization. The recent Maclean's
June 29, 1987

Decima poll on how Canadians feel about capital punishment specifically points out that religion does have a bearing on attitudes about the death penalty with Protestants in general, and Anglicans in particular, more likely to lean toward capital punishment while Catholics tend to lean toward the abolitionist point of view.
According to Michael M. Ferguson of Moncton: "The orthodox Christian tradition has generally emphasized three key points: First, the state has in principle the right, within limits and for good cause, to take life. Second, it is a question of prudence when and where the state should, if at all, exercise that right. Third, there is no definitive Christian position on the matter, and the individual, if properly informed, is free to make up his or her mind. The Jewish tradition does not appear to me to take a materially different position than orthodox Christianity, and in our own time the State of Israel retains the death penalty".
This is all to demonstrate that my own upbringing has contributed to a personal philosophy which is not out of line with my countrymen of similar backgrounds. This is not to say, as a Member of Parliament, that 1 cannot also demonstrate leadership and use my conscience and intelligence to operate independently from my traditional upbringing. My parents will confirm that I have gone that route many times before. This is, as many of my colleagues have expressed eloquently during this debate, a matter of conscience, a moral question, and I have analysed it in the way I have described.
My reason for supporting the motion tonight, while a "gut feeling" and a responsibility to my constituents, also amounts to something else, something far more immediate and urgent than the prospects of this country actually returning to executing people which, as I have already pointed out, will not likely happen.
My vote will be cast as a plea to this and future Governments to dramatically tighten up our parole system and our sentencing procedures. My Winnipeg friend, Frank Crockett, was quoted in Maclean's as saying, "If I had some assurance that a 25-year sentence meant 25 years, then I'd have no hesitation in saying, 'Don't bring back the death penalty'". Well, I am not as lenient as Mr. Crockett, but he does express the frustration of many of my constituents.
There is something fundamentally wrong with a system which allows a confessed murderer back out on the streets 24 or 30 months or three or five years after sentencing. As my mother said to me just this afternoon on the phone from Vancouver, "They're out in no time flat". A life sentence is a joke, Mr. Speaker. If we are not going to have capital punishment, we must build into the system a deterrent so the sentences given out for premeditated murder and the killers of police and prison guards and terrorists must be respected. We have heard during this debate that there are murderers in penal institutions who will kill again because they have nothing to lose. There are statistics to show that killers on parole will kill again.
Capital Punishment
It is my firmly-held belief that if this motion is defeated- and at this hour it could be even by the slimmest razor-thin margin-abolitionists will heave a sigh of relief and society will revert to the status quo. Canada's parole system will continue to make a mockery out of the administration of justice where first degree murderers are concerned. My view, my preference, is that with the death penalty once again on the statute books the sentencing of killers of police, prison guards, children, terrorists-whomever the committee selects to qualify for capital punishment-will have their sentences commuted to life imprisonment. Then a Government will be compelled to justify to the Canadian people that the lesser life sentence is respect and if not, why not.
Even if this motion is lost this evening, whichever way it goes, we as parliamentarians have a duty to ensure that one way or another we will bring an end to open season on those who protect society. In the interest of law and order, and as a grim and forceful reminder to would-be killers that the ultimate penalty is once again on Canada's statute books, I will be rising in my place later tonight to vote for the motion in principle to reinstate capital punishment.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from the outset I should like to say that I do not agree with the restoration of capital punishment, and even less with this resolution. I would also express my regret that this debate should even be taking place. I have no praise for the Prime Minister. The Elon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott) who has just spoken commended the Prime Minister for allowing a free vote on this issue. But why this vote? Why take up the time of the House for this useless debate? If, as suggested by the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth, we are not going to reinstate the death penalty, then why not instead debate the real and serious issues facing our society today?
Mr. Speaker, had we devoted as much effort to study the sources of violence in our society, we would be further ahead.
Here are some of the questions which deserve our attention. What should we do to improve our penitentiaries? What should we do to have better control over firearms? I have yet to see this Government take the lead in this respect. How can we reduce the violence we see on television every day? What can we do to gain better insight into family quarrels, alcohol and drug abuse?
These are questions we ought to debate, these are the kinds of problems whose solutions might help us reduce violence in our society.
At the beginning of my remarks I should like to thank all my constituents, particularly those who wrote to me about this mater. I received about ten personal letters and more than 150 postcards, all of them against capital punishment.
Therefore I think I can safely say that I share the views of at least some of the residents of my riding of Laurier.

I want to deal briefly with the question of public opinion. This question was addressed by a professor of criminal law at McGill University in an article published today in The Gazette.
I addressed the question of public opinion several weeks ago when I spoke to Bill C-55 dealing with the determination of refugees in Canada. In my speech on second reading I pointed out that the very first argument the Minister brought to bear in support of Bill C-55 was that public opinion supports Bill C-55. As Professor Sklar asked in The Gazette today: "How many have read Bill C-55? How many understand it?" While the legal community is unanimous about some of the provisions, their views widely contradict the views expressed by the Minister.
How many have carefully considered the arguments about the value of the death penalty as a deterrent? How many have reflected on the U.S. experience that the death penalty is applied in a disproportionate manner to minorities and the poor? What if public opinion changes? Do we invoke the death penalty one day and revoke it the next if the public's view changes?
I would also point out that majorities in Canada supported the internment of Japanese Canadians during the war. The majority of public opinion presumably supported keeping Jews out of Canada in the 1930s and 1940s, and presumably supports keeping out refugees today if one can believe the polls that have been published lately.
The real question is whether the public's views are the right answers to these questions, or do Members of Parliament have a different duty in dealing with these questions as part of our responsibility to the people who vote for us? In that respect, I would simply quote what Professor Sklar said about elected representatives in the last sentence of his article:
What we need, ultimately, is that they protect us from our prejudices, not legislate them.
In supporting the abolition of capital punishment in his speech to the House on June 15, 1976, Prime Minister Trudeau argued that the only basis to justify capital punishment is on its value as a deterrent. He said:
The crux of the question before us is whether execution is an effective and therefore justifiable weapon for the state to use in order to deter potential murderers.
In other words, is hanging a good way for society to defend itself? It may surprise some people in the House or the public to know that the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau said that capital punishment could be justified if there were evidence that executions were likely to deter other murders. This would ensure that a human life was not being taken capriciously. In other words, it would ensure that state-sanctioned killing would accomplish some worth-while social purpose. There was no such evidence in 1976 and there is no such evidence in 1987. Indeed, all the evidence is to the contrary.
As the Leader of our Party, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) said in his speech on April 27, even the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police no longer argues that capital punishment is the only effective deterrent. In the civilized world there is no evidence to show that capital punishment has had any significant impact on the murder rate. At 2.1 murders per 100,000 people, last year's homicides rate in Canada was the lowest in the past 15 years. It was 2.9 murders per 100,000 people in 1976 when capital punishment was abolished. If we look at the United States, we see its statistics show that those states which imposed the death penalty report a higher number of homicides than do other states where it has been abolished.
June 29, 1987

Like other Members of this House, I have had contact with the families of murder victims. One of the most difficult things I have had to do as a Member of Parliament was to meet with a certain Anibal Tavares, the father of a nineteen-year old student by the name of Emmanuel who was murdered in March, 1985 while resisting an armed robbery in the family's depanneur or convenience store in my constituency. This young man worked for me in the last election campaign. I went door to door with him.
The murderer in that case pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life imprisonment. He will be eligible for parole in 10 years.
I met with the Crown prosecutor after having met with the father on a few occasions and asked him a number of questions the father had put to me. He discussed with me the difficulties he faced in obtaining a conviction.
There was no witness to the crime. In the words of the Crown prosecutor, it was a perfect crime. However, the murderer talked to others who provided information to the police which led to his arrest. There was some question in the Crown prosecutor's mind whether this evidence would lead to a conviction. He was not sure whether the persons whom the murderer had talked to would turn up at the trial. They were not exactly reputable persons and there was no guarantee they would turn up. He also was not sure whether their testimony would hold up under cross-examination. His main objective was to get a murder conviction. He had to weigh the possibility of going to trial and not obtaining a guilty verdict because of the risky nature of that procedure versus obtaining a guilty plea by the accused prior to trial.
I met with Mr. Tavares, the father, on a number of occasions since his son's murder, as I explained. As can be expected, this man was absolutely shattered by his son's death. His anguish and his views have been reported several times by the city columnist of the Montreal Gazette who reported that Mr. Tavares lamented the death of moral principles, the death of justice in our society, and claimed that the state was responsible for his son's murder. The laws of the land, he argued, border on complicity, and the rules of evidence favour criminals. I guess I should not have to point out that Mr. Tavares also favours the death penalty. His views partially stem from the fact that his son's murderer was a person who had a lengthy criminal record. From 1980 to 1983, he had eight convictions from assault to break and enter and possession of stolen goods. As a young man he was convicted and sentenced to probation. His sentences increased to six months, nine months and 12 months in prison.
Mr. Tavares, in my mind, is fully justified in asking why this individual was on the street in a position to be able to murder his son. I believe that the previous record of this murderer testifies really to the failure of our criminal justice system. I do not mean to absolve this individual from responsibility for his actions. However, I think we have to recognize that prisons very often do not rehabilitate criminals. The prison system, on the contrary, probably often hardens criminals. A young man convicted of a relatively minor offence comes into contact with
Capital Punishment
hardened criminals and upon leaving prison perhaps is involved in a criminal world which leads to further and more serious crimes.
Prisoners, I am convinced, are often ill-prepared to return to society. I have met some convicts who have been released from prison and who have come to see me in my constituency office. They go on welfare because they have no training and very few support systems outside the prison world to help them to become independent again in our society. The care and attention which is given to victims of violence is undoubtedly inadequate.
Another question I could mention is that our criminal system, as was mentioned by the previous speaker, has undoubted weaknesses. There are many problems. Sentences are not proportional to offences. Punishment is not certain. We imprison far too many people, indeed, a much higher proportion than in other countries.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, if you followed a seminar which was organized for parliamentarians about two months ago which dealt with many of these problems in our criminal justice system. Unfortunately, that seminar was very poorly attended. I think there were only about five or six Members of Parliament who attended that particular seminar. Capital punishment will not solve these kinds of problems. Capital punishment, in my mind, is too simple an answer. It is an admission of failure. I have faith in the human spirit. I have confidence in our ability to take positive steps to protect human life and to reduce violence. I would suggest to Members of the House who may be wavering, if indeed there are any Members who are still wavering, that they consider the problems which have been raised in this debate. Yes, there is a need to reduce violence in our society, but I believe that if they reflect carefully on many of the difficulties we face in our prison system, and if they reflect carefully on the many types of things we could do to reduce violence, they must come to the conclusion that those alternatives are far better than returning to capital punishment and reinstituting a system under which violence can only beget further violence.
In conclusion, I would like to quote indirectly the parish priest in the Portuguese community in my constituency who spoke at the funeral of young Emmanuel Tavares. He stated that it was in the hands of young people in particular to do something about it, not to waste his life but to make it into something positive, to do something to prevent this kind of tragedy from happening again.
I am firmly convinced that it is in our hands. It is within our power and it is within the ken of Canadian society to deal with these issues and minimize violence in our society so that we see those kinds tragedies happen less often than they do at the present time.

June 29, 1987
Capital Punishment

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to say that my position on capital punishment was taken long ago and it is well-known to those who have known me since my early youth. It may be a matter of family upbringing or religious upbringing. It may be the kind of education I had in various classical colleges in Quebec. It may be the fact that I have been a member of the Bar since 1969 and have acted as defence counsel in criminal court for fifteen years, until my election as a Member of the House of Commons. In any case, it means that today, I cannot speak out in favour of this motion and will vote, without any reservations, against the motion and against capital punishment.
Mr. Speaker, from the very outset, I have tried to explain, without ever trying to hide them, my own views on capital punishment to my constituents. I asked them to write and tell me why they were for or against reinstatement of capital punishment-not that they would influence my own position, which was pretty firmly anchored, although you never know- to find out what their arguments were and to be able to give them the real facts. Many times in conversations with friends, associates, lawyers and some of my constituents, I realized that their opinions were based on facts that were inaccurate. And after our discussions, they would start wondering, and after a while, they would reverse their views.
I therefore asked my constituents to write to me. I received several hundred letters, and 820 or 86 per cent of my correspondents were against capital punishment, mostly for religious reasons. I told them I would send them a copy of the speech I would make today and some material we were sent by various agencies across Canada. I wrote to the others, who gave me their opinion based on facts that were often incomplete. Many wrote to me later to thank me for sending the material, and some actually changed their minds. That is one reason why in voting on this important issue, a Member should not be guided by the polls alone.
A poll is an attempt to find out what people think at a given moment, without providing information or making distinctions. We had 75 per cent of Canadians in favour of capital punishment only a few months ago, but this percentage has been coming down gradually, so that today, there would be 61 per cent. In Quebec, the last poll showed that a majority of Quebecers are now against capital punishment, probably because of the public debate that has taken place. If there had been a real referendum, if every Canadian citizen in each province had been able to vote personally for or against capital punishment, that citizen should have done what every Member has done, and that is, get the information, study the facts, read all the documents available, form an opinion and then vote. We would then have the real, enlightened view of Canadians. But since that process would have been very costly anyway and the Government chose to go through the House of Commons,
which is quite appropriate, a Member of Parliament has an obligation to vote according to his conscience, after carefully going over the facts.
I therefore do not share the view that Members of Parliament should vote according to surveys. Suggesting that is a false perception, a mistaken view.
When I state I received letters from constituents I have tremendous respect for, those letters reflected the same concerns that are now expressed in various analyses, the Maclean survey for instance which just appeared in June 1987. But certain analyses we saw, as reported in that excellent study The Death Penalty by The Criminal Lawyers' Association of Ontario, according to people generally, the general public perception is that 50 per cent of all crimes are violent. But the facts are different. It is not true to suggest that every second crime is violent in Canada. Only 8 per cent are. Those 8 per cent are a far cry from the public perception of 50 per cent. Two Canadians out of three believe the murder rate increased. That is wrong, the murder rate did not increase. Since 1976, when capital punishment was abolished in Canada, the murder rate declined from 3.09 per 100 000 citizens to 2.78 per 100 000. The rate declined since capital punishment was abolished in Canada. Those facts are self eloquent. Therefore, it is incumbent on those who believe capital punishment is a deterrent to prove it. The Prime Minister said so. They should prove that. The onus is on supporters of capital punishment to prove it would be a significant deterrent. But the facts, statistics point to the contrary.
How many times do I hear-and I am going to refer to police officers, and I will digress in my speech to refer to police officers. I followed very closely the contribution made by the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi) last Thursday. He was a police officer before he came to this House a few years ago, and he always supported capital punishment as a requisite in Canada, but now he just made a vibrant plea against reinstating capital punishment. I want to tell the Hon. Member for Bourassa that I admire his great courage. I admire his courage because personally, over these last few months, I had a number of opportunities to discuss the matter of capital punishment and I know the man's courage, his convictions. I listened to his speech, it does him honour. He will agree with me that statistics show the number of police officers killed in Canada has not increased since capital punishment was abolished.
Let us look at the years 1966 through 1975-in ten years, 38 police officers were killed in Canada. Let us now look at the ten following years: 37 were killed. So, since capital punishment was abolished, one police officer less has been killed, while the number of police officers doubled in Canada. So, abolishing capital punishment certainly has not resulted in more police officers being killed as such. Of course, police officers are there to protect our lives and property. This is why we respect and love them as such. But because he is a police officer, this is no reason to reinstate capital punishment. The rate of police officer deaths in the line of duty is far from being one of the highest in Canada. If we looked at statistics as such,
June 29, 1987

we would see that the mortality rate among police officers is in the vicinity of 9 per 100 000, as against 157 for fishermen, 119 for forestry workers, 83 in mining, 32 in the construction industry, for construction workers in our constituencies, etc.
Mr. Speaker, penalty is not a deterrent but rather the degree of certainty of being caught when committing a crime.
You are signaling that my time has almost expired. A number of Members want to speak. Well, I will skip a few things in my speech, Mr. Speaker, because I would like to refer to something of real significance to me, because of course I am directing my comments to my constituents, but also to Members in this Elouse who might not have a firm position as yet.
Capital punishment is not the solution. The solution is to prevent second offences. The solution is to ensure criminal rehabilitation. And the solution as such is to reduce the crime rate. And how do we go about that, Mr. Speaker? By reforming sentencing. Perhaps by making sentences more severe or by amending them to find a more adequate formula. Also by amending parole. And the Law Reform Commission suggested the Government should undertake such a study immediately. And the Commons Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General promised to study that as early as next fall. So it happens, Mr. Speaker, I defended people in murder cases and rape cases. I acted as consel for 74 defendants before jury in my professional life, and I can tell you that I was always surprised when a young guy 23, 24 came to my office with a record of convictions that long who just committed a robbery, and when I told him: OK, this might get you a few years in prison, his surprised look of anger shower he was thinking of seeing another lawyer.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, when you look at the record certain individuals have, you realize people do not become criminals overnight. They do not become murderers overnight. You will not find one individual who one day is pure as lamb and the next day will go and buy a gun and cartridges, load the gun, go to a bank and kill a guard or someone else. That is not the way it happens. Before that he appeared before judges. For a first offence, he raised a smile. For a second offence, he was committed to his parents. For a third offence, he was reprimended. For a fourth offence, he got a fine, then probation, then a second probation. Finally, for a seventh or eighth offence, the judge sentenced him to 60 days' prison to be done over weekends. Often this is where the young fellow is criminalized. He is simply criminalized. It is just as if as a society we put a gun in his hands.
And now you would like to hang that young fellow, you would like to send him to the electric chair. No. It is my view that there is a lot of alternatives in our society before we come to such a difficult solution. It may not solve all murders either. I hear some of my citizens suggest all murderers should be sentenced. There are crimes of passion. We know that some 80 per cent, I think it is over 80 per cent of people who commit murder as such kill someone who is close to them. A spouse, a
Capital Punishment
wife, a husband, a child. A friend, a neighbour. Somebody close. It is not an implacably planned and premeditated murder. This applies to the greater majority of murders. There are a great many solutions other than capital punishment to try and reduce the homicide rate in cases of this kind.
There is also the real amateur. The amateur does not think. He reacts immediately, spontaneously, as such. And he is often found by the courts guilty not of first degree murder, but of second degree murder. Therefore, not a murder punishable by the death penalty.
We are thinking therefore only of premeditated murders as such. I challenge anybody to find someone who has been found guilty of a planned and premeditated murder and who had no previous criminal record. I think that is where the solution lies. It is by working on sentencing, on rehabilitation and parole, making its conditions more severe.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians just cannot understand how a criminal who has been sentenced by a judge to 12 years in prison can obtain day passes after seven or eight months or be paroled after two years. They just cannot understand that. They do not find any reason for that. Criminals should get lighter sentences, but at least they should spend in prison three quarters of their sentences.
Canadians no longer understand the justice system. They can no longer make head or tail of it. Because of that, they are asking today for something which is worse, capital punishment, as though this was the universal remedy.
Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude immediately by saying that Canada has made tremendous efforts over the past few years-I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) who is here today could vouch for that-to serve as an example for all other countries in the world in the area of human rights. If we should reinstate capital punishment in this country, how would countries such as Iran, the U.S.S.R., all the other countries which violate human rights-I do not refer to these two countries in particular-would react when they find out that Canada had reinstated capital punishment?
Mr. Speaker, as a civilized nation, we have to be against capital punishment just as we were against flogging, quartering, against the use of the wheel and the garrotte. Mr. Speaker, an error is always possible: 79 per cent of Canadians agree that a judicial error is possible. And when we know that it would be possible to sentence to death an innocent, we should not take a chance.
Mr. Speaker, I strongly urge all my colleagues in the House to vote against reinstating capital punishment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to put my views with respect to the question of capital punishment on the record. And, of course, it is not the first time I have spoken on this issue, though it is

June 29, 1987
Capital Punishment
certainly the first time I have spoken in this Elouse on the issue. I spoke in a public forum in Winnipeg with regard to capital punishment. Members from all three political Parties were asked to attend and to address the issue of capital punishment, and I accepted on behalf of my Party to attend. There was a representative from the Liberal Party in attendance. Unfortunately, in that situation there was no representative of the Progressive Conservative Party.
I welcome the opportunity this evening to address this issue. The question that I think needs to be answered is: Why is this issue before us? Is it because there is an overwhelming case in favour of capital punishment? Is it that, after weighing all of the evidence for and against capital punishment, one comes logically and without a doubt to the conclusion that capital punishment is necessary in Canada? Or is it because of politics, because of public opinion polls, because of politics at leadership conventions?
I think that, really, is the question that we need to ask ourselves. We need to ask why it is that we are voting on this issue, and why it is we are voting on it at one o'clock in the morning. Why are we debating this issue deep into the dark of the night? Why can we not face up to this issue in the full light of day?
I want to deal with the question of whether there is a case for capital punishment on its merits, not in terms of public opinion polls or whether or not it is popular. I would like to look at its merits from a couple of basic perspectives. Will capital punishment work? Is it the right thing to do? Is it just? Is it moral? Is it principled? Then I will close my remarks by talking about how we are dealing with the issue and how it needs to be dealt with.
First I will turn to the question of whether it will work, whether it is something that will be effective. If we in the House choose to reinstitute the policy of capital punishment, will it be effective for society? Will it work? What will it do? If there is a case for capital punishment, it must be that somehow it will protect Canadians, that it will protect society, that it will make us more secure.
I have thought about an interesting question in this regard- are Canadians, in terms of their security, any worse off since the abolition of capital punishment? The statistics demonstrate that there has been no great rise in capital crimes following the abolition of capital punishment. There has been no great increase in the number of murders in our society, if we look at the facts, the statistics. That is one crucial question which I have asked myself.
Another way of looking at the question is: if capital punishment is reinstated, do our constituents really believe that three years or four years down the road they will be better off, that they will be more secure when they walk the streets, or that they will be subject to less violence? Common sense tells us, no. It would be a very pale ending to the motion before
the House if people really believed that with the reinstatement of capital punishment they would be more secure as they walked the streets of their neighbourhoods.
I return to the question of whether capital punishment will work and protect society. Will capital punishment affect the behaviour of people? Will it actually stop people from committing murder? If a punishment is to affect human behaviour, we must be certain that the punishment will be carried out consistently every time the crime is committed. A fundamental weakness with capital punishment is that it is an uncertain, indefinite, unsure, and unlikely punishment. If punishment is to affect behaviour, it must be certain.
The punishment is uncertain because juries are very reluctant to convict people of capital crimes when they know the punishment will be death. The juries, the people asked to carry out this punishment, hold back from imposing the final sentence and refuse to implement it. They convict people of lesser levels of crime. Common sense tells us that the existence of capital punishment will not provide society with greater protection.
I want to give another example of why capital punishment cannot work. Many of us are parents. Many of our constituents are parents. When we deal with children we know that they make a distinction between our words and our actions. We can tell children not to do something or we set down rules for them. However, if they do it and we turn our backs, we do not enforce the rule, they will not pay any attention to it because it does not affect their behaviour. If society establishes a rule that one who murders will be murdered and then does not carry it through, it has no impact, it does not affect behaviour, and therefore it does not protect society.
I would like to see a society in which people feel more secure when they walk the streets, are better protected, and are free from violence. Therefore, we must ask the following question: If capital punishment will not do that, are there other ways to arrive at that situation? Are there other ways to look at the question of violence in society? Are there other ways to look at the insecurity which people feel as they walk the streets?
I think there are more fundamental ways which require long-term work in order to achieve the result. Achieving a secure society in which people are free from violence is not a short-term effort. We should not be turned away by the fact that the process will be a long one.
There are things which we as a Parliament and as Canadians need to look at. We should be reviewing our policing policies. Is it effective to have police in inner cities in ridings like mine simply patrolling in automobiles? Would it make more sense and would senior citizens feel more secure if they had police on the beat, walking the streets and showing a presence? Would they feel greater security when they meet someone on the street who threatens them? We need to look at our policing patterns.
June 29, 1987

We need to look at the question of sentencing. We need a parliamentary debate in that regard. Many Canadians are alarmed when they see people convicted of brutal crimes and then hear about them walking the streets a very short period of time thereafter. We should enter into a very legitimate debate with regard to sentencing, and we could do it without going down the road of reinstating capital punishment.
We should also look at how parole is handled in society. There are policy areas which need to be examined without going down the wrong highway. At the same time, policing and sentencing do not take place in a vacuum. Certainly policing does not take place in a vacuum. I believe we need to look at our community development policies.
It is not enough to have a policeman driving a car or even walking the streets. For policing to be effective, it must take place in the context of a community. Many of our communities have been devastated by economic trends in society. We need effective community development policies so that we have genuine neighbourhoods, so that neighbours know each other, so that policing policies can operate within a community context.
We also need to look at social conditions which incubate violence. We need to look at how to eliminate poverty in society so that it does not become a breeding ground for violence. We should seek ways of building a better society. We should build a society upon co-operation rather than upon violence. I believe that the argument in favour of capital punishment falls down when we ask the question of whether it will work to protect society. We need to look at alternative wayr to build a secure security in which people are free from the fear of violence.
I come to the next question, namely, is capital punishment the moral thing to do? Is it the right thing and the just thing to do? My answer to that is no, because fundamentally it comes down to a question of values. What value does one place on human life? It is because I believe in the sanctity of human life that I think capital punishment, the taking of human life, is wrong. All of the great religions of the world teach that the taking of human life is wrong. If we ask the question of whether capital punishment is the right thing to do, I think our answer has to be, no.
Let us look at this from another perspective. Is this the moral or the right thing to do? If society chooses to kill people, if society chooses to impose the death penalty, or if society chooses to hang people, what kind of an example are we setting for members of society? What kinds of values are we teaching? I suggest the obvious, namely, that we are teaching disrespect for human life. We are teaching violence. We are teaching revenge. These are not the values that we wish to teach if we want to build a society based on moral values.
To decide whether this is the right thing and whether capital punishment is just and moral all we have to do is to look at
Capital Punishment
where we get the model for our own behaviour from. Where do we learn our own values and behaviour? Do we learn them from the great moral teachers of all time, from Jesus, from Mohammed and all of the great religious leaders? Or do we turn to a killer as the model for our own behaviour? Surely that will tell us whether capital punishment is the moral or the right thing to do.
Is capital punishment fair? Based on the statistics that exist in the United States, capital punishment is patently unfair because it falls much more heavily upon the minorities, the blacks and the visible minorities throughout the U.S. In Canada, I am not familiar with the statistics, but having checked into Canadian jails and penitentiaries, which are disproportionately filled with native people, who are a very small percentage of our society, it is clear to me that if we have capital punishment then the minorities, the native people, the blacks, and visible minorities will suffer this penalty disproportionately to those who are in the majority of society.
Another thing that concerns me is the possibility of error. Once one implements capital punishment, there is no way to reverse it. We know there are volumes of cases in the American experience in which juries and judges have made mistakes and imposed the wrong penalty. If one imposes the penalty of death, there is no way to reverse it. We already have some experience in Canada in which Canadian courts have made mistakes. Surely we do not want to fill our own volumes of books with irreversible mistakes.
Why are we dealing with this whole question of capital punishment? Is it because of the merits of the case or is it because of politics? Judging capital punishment on whether it works to protect society, capital punishment fails. I come to the conclusion that we are dealing with this question because of politics, because of the politics of a leadership convention. That was the way in which a future Prime Minister was able to get the votes in order to lead his Party. That is the politics with which we are dealing.

speechtext: That is a falsehood.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
We are also dealing with this matter because of the politics of polls. We have a governing Party that is at the bottom of the pit in the polls. Some Members of that Party see this matter as a way to recoup. I believe we are dealing with this issue because of politics.
How do we deal with this question? Do we deal with it as a matter of public opinion, of politics, or do we deal with it as a matter of personal conscience? I think the behaviour of juries demonstrates to us that it is a matter of personal conscience. When ordinary Canadians read about cases in newspapers, they tend to come to the conclusion that a person should be convicted. When they hear the evidence as a jury, they tend not to want to impose capital punishment. This tells me that the matter is one of conscience. Why ask Members of Parliament to do what juries will not do? Why ask Members of Parliament to do what Prime Ministers have refused to do?

June 29, 1987
Capital Punishment
This matter of capital punishment is a matter of conscience. We should deal with it accordingly and we should vote against its reinstatement.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the issue of capital punishment. It is a subject that has been debated now for many days. We have heard those who are for it and those who are against it. All sorts of arguments have been brought forward, arguments that are certainly valid in one instance and the other.
I listened to the speaker who preceded me who told us about the sanctity of human life. No doubt human life is extremely valuable. But because of its sanctity, nobody has the right to take it away. If a criminal kills somebody, there should be an adequate punishment for that deed. We hear the bleeding hearts saying that we should not take human life.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext: Like your Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON REINSTATEMENT
speechtext:
But the state has an obligation to preserve human life. The state does it by having a constitution. Section 7 of the Constitution tells us that we should preserve life, liberty and security of the person. For that reason, the state, as such, has an army to defend it from outside invasion to preserve democracy and it has a police force to preserve it internally. If somebody attacks the good order of government, he is violating some law. Naturally, taking somebody's life, whether it is for the state or for an individual, is a very serious offence, but the state, because it has to protect the individual, has the right to do so.
We can bring up all kinds of statistics for and against capital punishment. If I look at the year 1961, the rate of murders was 1.1 per 100,000 population. In 1962 the last execution took place. The Government gave the signal that it did not intend to apply the law. From 1962 to 1976 the rate increased to 2.81 per 100,000 population, it more than doubled.
The Government had given the signal that it would not apply the law of capital punishment. Once that signal was given, the number of crimes increased and we had to increase our police forces.
